He said he represented his school in all competitions, notably choir and singing, was nicknamed "the child with the golden voice", sang in the choir and instrumental ensemble at secondary school, was co-opted into the orchestra "Zaly Band", and was chosen at a national festival to come to Conakry as a solo singer for the Nzerekore federation; his father, a political official and member of the federal bureau, had him travel with the orchestra for safety.

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: On his idols: said the late Elhadj Sory Kandia Kouyate, with his beautiful voice, was his idol; that he loved the Sofas de Camayenne and the Syli Authentique with the voice of Yaya Bangoura in "Yerewolo", "Andree" and "Senero", voices that fascinated him and whose pieces he would cover; and that as a Christian the church choirs also inspired him - "music, in a word, is a matter of passion."

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: On difficulties at the start: said his father was a political official and member of the federal bureau of N'Zerekore, so there was no question of anyone in the family stopping him, especially during the Revolution when sport and theatre were included in education; he knew how to divide his time between studies and rehearsals and faced practically no opposition.

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: On the formation of the duo with Malick Conde: said they were work colleagues at the Patrice Lumumba printing house, that Conde was a former musician of the Dirou Band of Kindia, and that after hearing a radio announcement of a singing competition for the 2nd anniversary of the programme "Parade" hosted by journalist Louis Auguste le Roy, he proposed a song to Conde, they rehearsed for two days and recorded it, and he arrived at the national museum on the last day of submissions.

a3773.speaker: Louis Auguste le Roy, journalist and host of the programme "Parade"
a3773.speech: "... I regret to inform you that the closing has already taken place, and there are no more entries to be accepted, those are the competition rules..."

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: On the competition: said it took place in a venue near the 8 November cinema and gathered the emerging young performers of the moment, including "Boul Diallo", "Gaspari" and the group "Les Kamass"; that the duo "Philippe Kourouma-Malick Conde" won third prize, Gaspari second, and the orchestra Atlantique Melodie first; that it was his first time singing as an adult in a public place in the capital, that the emotion was great but he had rehearsed endlessly and Conde encouraged him, and that he charmed everyone with his voice; and that the piece was titled "Muso diyanan ko".

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: On performing solo: "It is a personal choice, an orientation decided in advance, a taste that is not up for debate. I think I express myself better acoustically than in an orchestra." He said he has never played a musical instrument but always manages to give the accompanying notes to his instrumentalists.

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: On his discography: said they never made albums but made recordings at RTG in Boulbinet, citing "Muso diyanan ko", "Aduna wela fi" and "N'na fanin tunun na"; that Malick Conde later returned to singing and guitar and performed "Temure" and "Salaya" in place of Seydouba; and that individually he was produced by "JMJ Music" of Justin Morel Junior on an 8-track album titled "Nu liba" in Guerze.

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: On commissioned compositions: said that between 1988-1989 the WHO asked Louis Auguste le Roy to find a group that could produce a composition on AIDS and the choice fell on them; that they were chosen to take part in the awareness caravan supporting and popularising Guinea's fundamental law and toured the country; and that they produced musical compositions on subjects such as "excision", "children's rights", "the environment", "Peace and reconciliation" with USAID-GUINEA, and "the fight against Ebola", as well as a song and video clip for the anniversary of the national radio (RTG).

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: On what he has to offer in the short term: said he is not very active but has just made a musical composition in a local studio and is gathering the human, technical, material and financial means to produce the video clip, for a song titled "Nene", a love song.

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: On his sources of inspiration: "Life is full of sources of inspiration... There is the social side, the natural side, everything that befalls me, that strikes me, that attracts me, and that touches my state of mind, gives rise in me to musical compositions."

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: On how he came to head SONOGUI: said he is a technician by profession and a musician as well, and RTG management needed someone with that profile; the choice fell on him through the confidence of Justin Morel Junior, then Director of RTG.

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: Describing SONOGUI: said it is made up of two sections, one for production and publishing and one for promotion and marketing, includes a recording studio, takes part in designing sounds for radio and television programmes and in the revaluation of national folklore; its mission is to lift up and encourage musicians who cannot afford private studios, in the image of the former Syliphone house, and to rehabilitate previously recorded but unbroadcast works whose preservation is lacking.

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: On results obtained: said several artists, theatre groups, musicians and ensembles recorded in their studio, citing "Lewru dyere", the "Zawagui", "Keletigui et ses Tambourinis" and the national instrumental ensemble; that they recorded the first album of "Rizo Bangoura" and produced many advertising spots.

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: On current difficulties: said they are going through difficult times that make activities rather unstable - first the air-conditioning problem, which took time and is now resolved, and also difficulties with equipment and a lack of personnel ; said they welcome the arrival of the new team at the supervising ministry, which through RTG management toured all the services to make contact and take stock of the difficulties in order to bring solutions, adding that they are optimistic and await the prompt reaction of the general management.

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: On projects to revive SONOGUI: said all projects revolve around means; that they had recommended, with the BGDA management, a project to recover all declared musical works but encountered difficulties; that they have planned a campaign to record folkloric works throughout the republic over 2 to 4 years, which would allow folkloric groups to be identified and recorded and their broadcast would encourage them; and that they had also planned the setting up of an RTG orchestra, which requires an operating budget to cover the musicians, noting they possess a batch of musical instruments given to them by LONAGUI.

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: Recounting memories: said that one day they were scheduled both on the Parade programme with Louis Auguste le Roy and at the 8 November cinema with the late Aly Badara Diakite, his Yamaha motorbike broke down, a taxi took them there with considerable delay, their singer Seydouba of the Djoliba Ballet had deserted them, but Malick Conde took up the hit "Temoure" with mastery - an unforgettable memory; and that during the awareness campaign around the fundamental law in Nzerekore the audience invaded the stage when he struck up the popular song "Zegbe Tutu", interrupting the show.

a3773.speaker: Philippe Kourouma, author, singer-songwriter and Director General of SONOGUI
a3773.speech: On his ambitions: "My ambition is to take some time in the company of Malick Conde, in order to re-record certain titles from our various repertoires. And that presupposes the choice of a studio of perfection, because we want, for posterity, that in images and in sound, all that public which knew us, and even those who do not know us, may remember us through our works."

a3840.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a3840.speech: Praised the leadership of His Majesty King Mohammed VI in promoting regional and international peace and security, and, in a statement released Monday in Washington following a telephone conversation with Nasser Bourita, underlined the importance of the Moroccan-American strategic partnership for regional and international peace and security ; Expressed the United States' desire to intensify cooperation with Morocco in order to advance common interests in the region and to end conflicts, notably within the framework of the Abraham Accords.

a3840.speaker: US State Department spokesperson (statement)
a3840.speech: Said the discussions between the two parties also covered the implementation of the Gaza ceasefire agreement, the release of the hostages, as well as Morocco's leadership in delivering humanitarian aid to the Palestinians.

a3840.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State, and Nasser Bourita, Moroccan Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation and Moroccans Residing Abroad
a3840.speech: Stressed the importance of strengthening trade and investment between the two countries for the benefit of the two peoples, according to the State Department statement.

a3867.speaker: Chafari Kanya Hanawa, Director-General of the West African Gas Pipeline Authority (Agao)
a3867.speech: Explained the work of her Authority and its commitment alongside the governments of the countries it covers; recalled that it is an international institution created by the Gao Treaty to represent the four States parties and to facilitate and regulate the pipeline; explained that she is travelling to make her institution known, its usefulness and the support it provides to States.

a3867.speaker: Chafari Kanya Hanawa, Director-General of the West African Gas Pipeline Authority (Agao)
a3867.speech: “Since 7 February, there have been disruptions in the gas supply. These disruptions are due to the fact that the pipeline had to be shut down in order to carry out maintenance operations. These operations lasted a month and have been completed for a few days now. Gas is flowing again towards the Maria-Gleta power plants for the production of electricity.” ; “As the regulator, we came to observe that the works are effective and completed, to reassure the population that this was planned maintenance intended to guarantee the integrity of the network and therefore the continuity of service.” ; “Activities have resumed, the system is operational...”

a3867.speaker: Agao officials (Alain Sedjro Houha, technical director; Peter Danlodi, director of administration and legal affairs; Yao Iroko, director of the environment; Hamis Ussif Mohammad, director of market surveillance and development)
a3867.speech: “The West African Gas Pipeline Authority was established to regulate the activities of the company in charge of operations, to represent the States on matters relating to the West African gas pipeline, and to facilitate the completion and extension of this project, in order to guarantee the States parties natural gas so as to enable them to produce electricity from this natural gas, which is an abundant resource in our region,” they specified. They also highlighted the potential of each country and the importance of the West African gas pipeline for sub-regional development.

a3867.speaker: Agao experts
a3867.speech: Concluded that the conditions under which the maintenance operation was conducted leave no room for doubt.

a3867.speaker: Agao delegation (the team)
a3867.speech: Will address the sector's authorities “to ask for their support for the continuity of actions in order to improve energy production in Benin and in the other countries.”

a3880.speaker: Raphael Morav, Israeli Ambassador to Ethiopia
a3880.speech: On the 75th anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz: "It was the International Day for the commemoration of the victims of the Holocaust. Although it is 75 years since the Auschwitz extermination camp was liberated, the issue of Holocaust is still very relevant today... The most important lesson of the holocaust is that violence starts with words; therefore, when we hear discourses of racist attitudes and heinous speeches of hatred and anti-Semitism, bigotry and such negative things, we have to be vigilant." ; "Violence starts with words and then it becomes acts of violence that may end in genocides and other horrible acts. That's the important lesson of the Holocaust. The world stood still 75 years ago when the Holocaust took place, and we thought it would never happen again, yet we regretfully saw several genocides in the world in Cambodia in the 70s and in Rwanda 25 years ago, so it means that it can still happen. Therefore, we need to be vigilant and act beforehand." ; "Today, we still hear anti-Semitic speeches, we see in some eastern European countries glorification of anti-Semites and people who actually cooperated with Nazi Germany in the Holocaust, so all these are alarming signs that really call for all civilized people to act." ; "I am a strong believer in education, because we are talking about a generation that was born long after the war... So I think education is the key to prevent future acts of this kind. At the same time, politically speaking, when we hear discourse of hatred and anti-Semitism, bigotry we need to take action, to say this will not continue, we will not allow such expression to be tolerated."

a3880.speaker: Raphael Morav, Israeli Ambassador to Ethiopia
a3880.speech: On reports that Israeli student trips to Ethiopia were suspended: "It's rather wrong information that I saw on the press. It was suggesting that the Ministry of Education of Israel is suspending trips of students from Israel to Ethiopia and this is incorrect. What is true is that there is a travel advisory to Ethiopia that calls for Israeli citizens to refrain from unnecessary trips to the Somali region and the Somali region only." ; "That is due to a potential threat of Al-Shabaab terrorist activities against Israeli nationals. It's my government's responsibility to its citizens to warn when there is a potential threat. It was maybe wrongly interpreted as a ban on trips to Ethiopia and this is definitely not the case. On the contrary, we encourage Israelis to visit Ethiopia, invest in the country and make business with Ethiopians partners." ; "Next Monday, I am receiving 35 youths who are coming to Ethiopia from Israel. We call it a 'Roots Trip' because they will be in the footsteps of the Beta Israel heritage."

a3880.speaker: Raphael Morav, Israeli Ambassador to Ethiopia
a3880.speech: On Israeli investment in Ethiopia: "Israeli investments in Ethiopia are mainly in the agricultural sector; normally many of them are private farms that have developed new varieties in Ethiopia. For example, one farm has introduced strawberries in Ethiopia, something that did not exist before... Today it's a huge exporter of strawberries from Ethiopia to all over the world." ; "We have another Israeli farm, which is growing chives, it is one of the biggest producer of chives in the world and again 98% of the production is for worldwide export." ; "This is the type of investment we are encouraging because they contribute not only to the economy of Ethiopia in terms of employment and transformation of agriculture but as well as they are all important exporters who are also bringing hard currency to Ethiopia which is very important for the economy." ; "Beyond investment, it's worth mentioning that the biggest drip irrigation project in the world is in Ethiopia conducted by an Israeli company Netafim... It's a big operation worth over $200 million."

a3880.speaker: Raphael Morav, Israeli Ambassador to Ethiopia
a3880.speech: On the hybrid seed/avocado project with USAID: "We have a very important project of cooperation in development with the Ministry of Agriculture and USAID that has been running for 13 years, for the introduction of high quality varieties of avocado. Today, thanks to this project, Ethiopia is an exporter of avocado fruits to Europe and there is now a pretty good know how of how to grow avocado of these varieties from the nursery to the whole value chain of production up to export." ; "We have set up six nurseries for avocado seedlings in Ethiopia that are producing over half a million seedlings per year and in addition to that, thanks to our encouragement, the private sector is now entering this activity and already produces about half a million more seedlings... It is really making a transformation in the agricultural sector of Ethiopia because it became the most profitable crop in Ethiopia, more than coffee or sesame or any other traditional crop."

a3880.speaker: Raphael Morav, Israeli Ambassador to Ethiopia
a3880.speech: On the restoration of a Jewish cemetery in northern Ethiopia: "There has been a Jewish presence in Ethiopia for about 2000 years and the Jews lived very closely with their Christian and Muslim neighbors, mostly in good relations... They are coming back to Ethiopia to visit the places and the people that they left." ; "An Israeli organization 'Matasabia' (remembrance) decided to restore all the places of the Beta Israel heritage in Ethiopia... their initiative is to create a 'Beta Israel trail' that will present and preserve the heritage sites of Beta Israel." ; "The first thing that they decided to do is to restore an old and important Jewish cemetery in Dabat area in the Amhara region. This cemetery, that I have visited, was serving 24 Beta Israel villages in the area and I found that it in a rather good condition... The good surprise was that the authorities that were there, the governor of the region, the mayor and other authorities all say that this is also part of Ethiopia's heritage; it's not just Beta Israel."

a3880.speaker: Raphael Morav, Israeli Ambassador to Ethiopia
a3880.speech: Summing up Ethiopia-Israel bilateral relations: "I would say the relations are very good, maybe even excellent. We are aiming higher and there is space to deepen and reinforce the relations. Politically speaking we had the exchange of visits at the highest level. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed visited Israel in September, the President of the State of Israel visited in May 2018, the Prime Minister of Israel visited in 2016... so politically speaking we have very open and close relations." ; "These political relations are translated into good economic relations; we are encouraging and working to bring more investment from Israel to Ethiopia... Last but not least, we are excited that Ethiopia will have, for the first time, free and fair democratic elections. We are supportive of this process of political reforms as well as the economic and social ones. I am convinced the future is even more promising."

a3918.speaker: Ethiopian government (by its own admission)
a3918.speech: By the government's own admission, the macroeconomic reality for Ethiopia is distressing.

a3918.speaker: National Bank of Ethiopia (central bank first-quarter report)
a3918.speech: The first-quarter report recently released by the central bank gives clarity on why inflation is pushing consumers to a breaking point: federal government revenue mobilisation declined by a tenth, to 73 billion Br compared to the same period in the previous fiscal year, while expenditures ballooned by just over a quarter, to 111.3 billion Br, leaving a fiscal deficit five times higher than at a similar period in the previous year; import bills ballooned by nearly a fifth, reaching 4.1 billion dollars, over four times export revenues, with fuel surging by 80pc; the balance of payments now has a deficit of 972 million dollars, five times as high as in the same period in the previous fiscal year; the central bank shelled out 113.5 billion Br to finance the federal government in the first quarter, 266.1pc more than the same period last year; and the broad money supply has climbed by more than a quarter.

a3918.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a3918.speech: Urges Ethiopia's authorities that prudent behaviour would be a broad money supply growth rate 10 percentage points lower than the more-than-a-quarter increase recorded.

a3929.speaker: UNAIDS
a3929.speech: Has announced a dramatic price reduction for lenacapavir, a revolutionary HIV prevention drug, described as a watershed moment for global health; the announcement, made on Tuesday during the United Nations General Assembly, detailed two agreements slashing the cost of lenacapavir from USD 28,000 per patient per year to just USD 40.

a3929.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, UNAIDS Executive Director
a3929.speech: “This is a watershed moment. A price of USD 40 per person per year is a leap forward that will help unlock the revolutionary potential of long-acting HIV medicines” ; noted that 1.3 million people were infected with HIV in 2024, far exceeding the 2025 target of 370,000 ; “UNITAID, Gates, CHAI, Wits RHI, Reddy, and Hetero have shown what is possible when companies prioritise equitable access to lifesaving medicines. Gilead must match this ambition by reducing its price for lenacapavir, being transparent on cost and pricing, expanding its generics licence to all low and middle-income countries, and enabling rapid access for more people in developing countries.”

a3929.speaker: The PURPOSE 2 Trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine
a3929.speech: Found lenacapavir 96 to 100 per cent effective in preventing new HIV infections.

a3929.speaker: UNAIDS (estimates)
a3929.speech: Estimates that access for 20 million high-risk individuals, including men who have sex with men, sex workers, people who inject drugs, and young women and adolescent girls in sub-Saharan Africa, could significantly reduce infections and advance the goal of ending AIDS by 2030.

a3929.speaker: Mduduzi Matsebula, Eswatini Health Minister
a3929.speech: Welcomed the development, calling it timely for Eswatini. “We support the reduced pricing for this important commodity in the fight against HIV. This ensures the government can roll it out to all who need it. One of our vulnerabilities has been the persistently high rate of new infections among women of childbearing age, and this will help us turn this trend around.”

a3929.speaker: Dr Nondumiso Ginindza-Ncube, NERCHA Executive Director, and Ntsika Fakudze, NERCHA Board Chairman
a3929.speech: Described the breakthrough as a game-changer for HIV prevention globally.

a3929.speaker: Dr Nondumiso Ginindza-Ncube, NERCHA Executive Director
a3929.speech: “As a country, we are looking forward to its launch during World AIDS Day on December 1 and have it ready for roll-out in January. Through UNAIDS, we have been promised about USD 660 000 (approximately E11.8 million) for a start, which is likely to benefit about 16 000 Emaswati” ; added that PEPFAR has pledged further funding to support the programme ; noted that Eswatini has been prioritised for the drug, with rollout guidelines being developed with the World Health Organisation ; “Emaswati were either taking medications daily or monthly. Now, they will only need two injections per year at a lower cost per patient.”

a4064.speaker: Grand Duke of Luxembourg
a4064.speech: Recalled his first visit to Cape Verde ten years ago, describing it as one of the best experiences of his reign ; "Cape Verde has become a model of stability in its region and an internationally respected nation. Its solid economic and democratic institutions make your country a point of reference. This year, 2025, also marked the 25th anniversary of my reign." ; "During this quarter century, Luxembourg has had the pleasure of accompanying Cape Verde. Indeed, our cooperation, begun in the 1990s, illustrates what two small nations united by the same ways can achieve." ; referred to the Cape Verdean community in Luxembourg, present for around 60 years, whom he called a bridge between the two peoples: "Their contribution to our two societies reinforces our admiration" ; told Cape Verdean youth that they are the guardians of this collective memory (independence) and responsible for overcoming today's challenges with intelligence, responsibility and determination.

a4064.speaker: Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa, President of Portugal
a4064.speech: Highlighted Cape Verde's commitment to the rule of law, respect for human rights and the regular functioning of democratic institutions ; said he was grateful and had admiration for and confidence in the country's promising future, fraternally saluting the Cape Verdean path since independence ; stressed that Cape Verde has followed a road marked by political maturity and is today a point of reference among the democracies of the African continent ; structured his message around six key words, among which he highlighted solidarity, recognition and gratitude: "Third word, recognition of your intelligence, knowing how to use our common language (...), but also knowing how to enrich it with your creoles, joining a language that is a universal platform between oceans, continents and peoples with a language of its own affirmation and nonconformity" ; evoked the historical ties between Portugal and Cape Verde and the capacity of the two peoples to transform complex relations into genuine closeness and cooperation ; concluded on a note of hope, affirming that Cape Verdean youth represent the certainty of a solid future for the country, which is prepared to face the next 50 years.

a4064.speaker: Amina Mohammed, United Nations Deputy Secretary-General
a4064.speech: Said that 5 July is an occasion to celebrate not only the shared past, but also the commitment to a fairer, more humane future for all ; underlined the importance of remembering the foundations of the United Nations Charter: "Today we are UN80 and we really need to remember why the Charter exists," noting that many of the organisation's principles are mirrored in the constitutions of post-independence African countries.

a4064.speaker: Amina Mohammed, United Nations Deputy Secretary-General
a4064.speech: Regarding Cape Verde's progress, pointed to the advances recorded over recent decades, with emphasis on health and education, citing the reduction of the maternal mortality rate from 112 to around 11 per 100,000 births: "In my country that number was once 1,200, and we are still at 500 or 600. To see these results here is something extraordinary."

a4064.speaker: Amina Mohammed, United Nations Deputy Secretary-General
a4064.speech: On the future of international cooperation, argued for a change of paradigm, considering that the traditional model of foreign aid should be replaced by investment in human development and climate action: "We still need support, but with a new mentality: investment in humanity. It is necessary to respond to the aspirations of countries and not to apply standardised solutions" ; said the future lies in more honest partnerships based on mutual listening and on valuing national visions: "Many of our countries today have very clear visions and are moving forward with or without us. And it would be better if they moved forward with us."

a4133.speaker: Football Association of Malawi (FAM) (press statement)
a4133.speech: Says the champions will receive K9 million; runners-up K5 million; 3rd placed K3 million and the 4th-placed side K2 million — with individual prizes being K200,000 each for the Top Goal Scorer, Player of the Tournament and the Best Coach; other incentives include each of the eight qualifying teams receiving a subvention of K1.5 million during the quarterfinals, K1.5 million each for the four semifinalists, while the three teams in the play-offs will receive a subvention of K800,000 each.

a4133.speaker: Ascent Soccer’s website
a4133.speech: According to Ascent Soccer’s website, Chinzimu is already garnering significant attention from Europe after turning 18 years of age in February.

a4144.speaker: Bass Sankhen, Senegalese sheep seller
a4144.speech: Described this year’s market as the most disappointing yet. “Last year was far better,” Sankhen said. “This year, the business is not working. The sheep are expensive, and the taxes are too high. I urge the government to reduce taxes so we can lower prices.”

a4144.speaker: Alieu Jobe, Gambian trader who sources sheep from Senegal
a4144.speech: Noted a marked hesitation among buyers. “People say they don’t have money, or they don’t have space to keep a ram until Eid,” Jobe explained. “Many are waiting until the day before to buy, hoping for lower prices.”

a4144.speaker: Jahjerry Bah, Senegalese trader
a4144.speech: Spoke of rampant theft plaguing the markets. “Thieves come at night and steal our sheep,” he said. “If you confront them, they’re ready to fight. I borrowed money to buy these sheep and need to sell them to pay it back. We need security here until the sales are done.”

a4144.speaker: Lamin Fofana, ram buyer
a4144.speech: “I was told D21,000 to D38,000 for sheep that aren’t even big,” he said. “I’ll wait until the day before Eid when prices might drop.”

a4144.speaker: Abubakar Faye, prospective buyer
a4144.speech: Pointed to the weak Gambian dalasi as a root cause. “Our currency is too weak against the CFA,” Faye said. “The government needs to strengthen the dalasi and enforce a policy to use only our currency in markets as other countries do.” ; also shared security concerns, noting a recent theft in his neighbor’s compound: “No one feels safe. I’m checking prices early, but I won’t buy until Thursday.”

a4253.speaker: Portuguese government
a4253.speech: Issued a note of caution regarding a matter which, whenever it is raised, proves delicate and complex.

a4253.speaker: World Bank (report on human capital development presented Monday)
a4253.speech: May establish that out of the total years of schooling “there are almost four years during which children do not manage to acquire the expected learning” and recommend “a learning environment with teachers speaking more Portuguese in the classroom”; according to the same report, with a relatively low human capital index the country may be losing 1.3% of future economic growth.

a4253.speaker: Reporters Without Borders
a4253.speech: Point out that the greater evil lies in the self-censorship of journalists, deriving in part from the dominant position of the public media organs.

a4253.speaker: Aristides Pereira, former President of the Republic of Cabo Verde (1988)
a4253.speech: Acknowledged that the “labour-intensive public works fronts (FAIMO) were the place where the industrious conscience of the people was degraded.”

a4471.speaker: Joint study by the International Air Transport Association (IATA) and Oliver Wyman, ‘Reviving the Commercial Aircraft Supply Chain’
a4471.speech: Estimates that the slow pace of global airplane production will cost the aviation industry more than US$11 billion in 2025; addresses supply chain challenges in the aerospace industry and explores the root cause of these challenges, the impact on airlines, and initiatives to move the industry forward; identified four main factors that will cost the industry billions this year – excess fuel costs, additional maintenance costs, increased engine leasing costs and surplus inventory holding costs; outlines key initiatives for OEMs, lessors and suppliers supported by airlines to confront the supply-demand imbalance and build greater resilience.

a4471.speaker: International Air Transport Association (IATA)
a4471.speech: Indicated that in 2024 passenger demand increased by over 10%, exceeding the capacity expansion of 8.7% and pushing load factors to a record 83.5%.

a4471.speaker: Willie Walsh, IATA’s Director General
a4471.speech: “Airlines depend on a reliable supply chain to operate and grow their fleets efficiently. Now we have unprecedented waits for aircraft, engines and parts and unpredictable delivery schedules. Together these have sent costs spiralling by at least US$11 billion for this year and limited the ability of airlines to meet consumer demand. There is no simple solution to resolving this problem, but there are several actions that could provide some relief. To start, opening the aftermarket would help by giving airlines greater choice and access to parts and services. In parallel, greater transparency on the state of the supply chain would give airlines the data they need to plan around blockages, while helping OEMs (original equipment manufacturers) to ease underlying bottlenecks.”

a4471.speaker: Matthew Poitras, partner in Oliver Wyman’s Transportation and Advanced Industrials practice
a4471.speech: “Today’s aircraft fleet is larger, more advanced, and more fuel efficient than ever before” ; “However, supply chain challenges are impacting airlines and OEMs alike. We see an opportunity to catalyse an improvement in supply chain performance that will benefit everyone, but this will require collective steps to reshape the structure of the aerospace industry and work together on transparency and talent.”

a4547.speaker: Young boy met at the hospital (aged eight)
a4547.speech: Mentioned that he was eight years old.

a4547.speaker: The boy's mother (mother of six, Sidist Kilo, Addis Abeba)
a4547.speech: Confirmed that her boy was indeed eight years old and that he has lived all his life in Addis Abeba, though he had not started school yet; said she, her husband and six children live in a one-room house in Sidist Kilo, and that she had come to the hospital seeking fertility treatment; said she had lost three children before they even reached five years of age.

a4547.speaker: Doctors (who treated the woman's children)
a4547.speech: Had told her that the primary cause of her three children's deaths was malnutrition.

a4547.speaker: UNICEF
a4547.speech: According to UNICEF, about a third of all child deaths are connected to malnutrition in Ethiopia, putting Ethiopia sixth in the global ranking of under-feeding its child population, with 72pc of these deaths preventable if malnutrition were halted.

a4547.speaker: USAID
a4547.speech: According to USAID, out of Ethiopia's 15.2 million children under the age of five, 38pc are severely stunted, while a quarter are underweight.

a4547.speaker: Medical professionals (estimates)
a4547.speech: Estimate that over half of Ethiopia's adult population is malnourished.

a4660.speaker: Daily Trust (report)
a4660.speech: Had reported how 76 protesters who were arrested during the August 1 to August 10 #EndBadGovernance demonstration were brought to a Federal High Court in Abuja, on Friday.

a4660.speaker: Coalition of Northern Groups (CNG), statement by national coordinator Comrade Jamilu Aliyu Charanchi
a4660.speech: Said the “detention and arraignment of those frail, malnourished and hapless children have exposed the government as a desperate entity that is determined to de-market and embarrass Nigeria before the international community while presenting its credentials for medals in gross inhumanity.” ; “The continued detention and mistreatment of these minors is a gross violation of their basic rights, including the right to freedom of expression and assembly. CNG strongly condemns this abuse of power and the blatant disregard for the welfare and dignity of young citizens.” ; “The treatment these children are receiving highlights a troubling failure of state actors to prioritize the welfare and rights of its most vulnerable citizens, children, especially when their ‘crime’ was to demand better governance and accountability.” ; “It is disheartening that in a country with a history of resilience and promise, minors are being made to endure starvation and harsh conditions while awaiting trial for daring to speak up for their future. This is not only a violation of domestic law but also contravenes international human rights principles protecting children from harm and unlawful detention.” ; “Ideally, those children are supposed to be treated first as victims of state abuse and deprivation whose leaders have failed to provide the necessary leadership that can mold them into better members of the society as they are a direct outcome of our decayed system.” ; “It is shamefully despicable that criminals and bandits that are holding the entire country to ransom do not face such stringent consequences for their actions.”

a4660.speaker: Coalition of Northern Groups (CNG), statement by national coordinator Comrade Jamilu Aliyu Charanchi
a4660.speech: On government economic policy: “Evidently, the Government has consistently proven that people’s problems and deteriorating situations are not part of its priority because of its disregard for the daily hardships of its citizens. Increasingly, frequent blackouts have become a norm across the country, severely impacting homes, businesses, and essential services which became worse with the recent blackout.” ; “The elimination of fuel subsidies and constant raising of fuel prices have pushed the cost of living to record highs, making basic necessities even harder to afford. Instead of prioritizing the welfare of the populace by providing feasible alternatives or relief, the government’s priorities appear to be detaining, abusing and crushing the vulnerable children that need support and protection to grow into responsible adults.” ; “Unfortunately, hunger and starvation have become weapons against defenseless and malnourished teenagers. It is clear that the government’s neglect of essential services and its catastrophic economic policies have strangulated millions in a state of uncertainty, desperation, and disillusionment in which these minors belong. These children must not be targeted as the scapegoat for expressing their frustrations as Nigerians have never gone through such dehumanizing and cruel policies that this administration promotes.”

a4660.speaker: Coalition of Northern Groups (CNG) (statement)
a4660.speech: Called for the immediate and unconditional release of all the minors detained for participating in the protests: “We demand that the government prioritize dialogue and constructive engagement over intimidation, especially with young citizens who represent the future of this nation.” ; “In the interim, we urge relevant agencies and civil society organizations to provide immediate humanitarian assistance to these detained children to mitigate further health risks. The protection of children is non-negotiable, and we implore the authorities to treat these young citizens with the compassion and respect they deserve.”

a4862.speaker: Myss Belmonde Dogo, Ivorian Minister of National Cohesion, Solidarity and the Fight against Poverty
a4862.speech: Receiving the donation on behalf of the Ivorian government, praised the excellence of the diplomatic relations between the two countries, and then affirmed that these dates would be distributed to the entire Ivorian Muslim community in order to support them during this period of fasting and reflection.

a4862.speaker: Saudi diplomat (Saudi ambassador to Cote d'Ivoire, unnamed)
a4862.speech: In his address, highlighted the depth of the historical ties between Saudi Arabia and Cote d'Ivoire, strengthened in recent years by increased cooperation in various fields; he recalled in particular the exchanges of official visits, the Kingdom's support through the Saudi Fund for Development in the area of infrastructure, as well as the humanitarian assistance provided by the King Salman Centre for Relief and Humanitarian Aid.

a4968.speaker: Huguette Bokpè Gnacadja, human rights and gender consultant and newly elected coordinator of Wildaf-Bénin
a4968.speech: On the value of the centre: said the phenomenon of violence remains intimately bound up with tradition and that the first reflex of any woman who has suffered such violence is to keep silent, a reflex reinforced by the reception given at police stations and gendarmerie brigades to matters regarded as "family" ones; said reporting amounts for women to an obstacle course, with people saying "it's a family matter, let's drop it" simply to dissuade victims, and that even in court the complexity of the procedure and the jargon used are foreign to them; said studies, surveys and analyses have shown that victims are more inclined to report when they find themselves in a more favourable, more supportive and more humane environment; said it was in that spirit that the 2012 law on the prevention and punishment of violence against women provided for centres for the care of victims of violence, that Benin now has two (Abomey, opened in 2014, and Cotonou), and that "Wildaf-Bénin had the idea of taking advantage of this requirement of the law and drew up a project which met with the agreement and the support of USAID"; said the centres serve to offer victims all the expertise and services they need in one place, so that they do not become discouraged travelling between the police station and the hospital, the objective being to create a framework favourable to women reporting.

a4968.speaker: Huguette Bokpè Gnacadja, human rights and gender consultant and newly elected coordinator of Wildaf-Bénin
a4968.speech: Said the opening of the care centres is a measure implementing the law, which only applies once its content has been sufficiently absorbed by those to whom it is supposed to apply; said the purpose of the centre is also to educate — it does not have a curative function or a function of preparing for punishment, but an educational function which, during the dialogues and discussions established between the victim and the perpetrator, will make people aware — and that through this grassroots education "we will gradually contribute to an application of the law in a context where it is understood even if it is not accepted."

a4968.speaker: Huguette Bokpè Gnacadja, human rights and gender consultant and newly elected coordinator of Wildaf-Bénin
a4968.speech: On what has changed since the first centre opened in Abomey in 2014: said "We note more and more the birth of the reflex. When victims discover that there is a place where they can find a solution to their concerns, it is a double encouragement for them. And when that place above all has a one-stop service desk, reporting is spontaneous"; said that at the very beginning turnout was low but by word of mouth people began to appreciate what is at stake in reporting, that a person close to the victim can take the step before she herself becomes involved, and that this reflex will necessarily curb the propensity to commit violence.

a4968.speaker: Huguette Bokpè Gnacadja, human rights and gender consultant and newly elected coordinator of Wildaf-Bénin
a4968.speech: On the current state of affairs: said that if one confined oneself to the current situation one could be discouraged, given the amount of violence committed against women and girls, but that "the situation is not brilliant but it has evolved" — from a time when it was not talked about at all to a phase in which they are listened to and the population knows that what they do has a criminal connotation and supports them; said the wall of silence has been broken and, although resistance is still present, the reflex of reporting and the awareness have been born, "and I think that is already a big step."

a4968.speaker: Huguette Bokpè Gnacadja, human rights and gender consultant and newly elected coordinator of Wildaf-Bénin
a4968.speech: On male victims: said "In the same way that we want to put an end to impunity with regard to women, we cannot cultivate it with regard to men"; said violence against men is increasingly developing and is characterised by two profiles of women perpetrators — those who act after reaching a point of exasperation or in response to violence they suffer, and those suffering from psychological disorders, alcoholism or drug addiction; said the care centres are also intended to serve men who are victims of violence and that cases of reciprocal violence will also be received, the aim being to strengthen families, without standing in the way of punishment where the situation calls for it; said the phenomenon is still played down because it has not reached an advanced degree, that the same sociocultural burdens account for it, and that very few men have the courage to say they have been beaten by their wives.

a5110.speaker: Lejone Mpotjoane, Lesotho Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5110.speech: Expressed his regret following US President Donald Trump's remarks about the country, inviting him to come and visit it ; responded on Wednesday, calling those statements "totally insulting" ; "I am truly shocked that my country should be described in this way by the President of the United States" ; "Lesotho is an important and unique country, and I would be happy to invite the president, as well as the rest of the world, to come and discover it."

a5110.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5110.speech: During his speech before the US Congress on Tuesday, had described Lesotho as a nation "that nobody has ever heard of," while criticizing US foreign aid spending, referring to an eight-million-dollar LGBTQ+ programme in Lesotho.

a5110.speaker: Lejone Mpotjoane, Lesotho Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5110.speech: Acknowledged that American aid supported various sectors in Lesotho, such as health and agriculture, and stressed that the cuts in health aid had had a considerable impact at a time when the government is trying to achieve self-sufficiency.

a5158.speaker: Elon Musk, head of the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge)
a5158.speech: Denied leading a “hostile takeover” of the US government and defended his cost-cutting plans; described sweeping government cuts as “common sense” measures that are “not draconian or radical” ; “The people voted for major government reform and that’s what the people are going to get. That’s what democracy is all about.” ; “I fully expect to be scrutinised. It’s not like I think I can get away with something.”

a5158.speaker: Democrats
a5158.speech: Have criticised the agency and accused it of a lack of transparency.

a5158.speaker: Federal judge (court ruling)
a5158.speech: Has blocked Doge from accessing treasury records – in a case that seeks to ensure the agency does not interfere with funding signed off by Congress, which is outside Doge’s scope.

a5183.speaker: Moumina Okieh Jireh, President of the IFTIN association
a5183.speech: Recalled the vital importance of the project, which will allow dozens of households access to drinking water — a programme that will spare the vulnerable women and girls of the neighbourhood concerned the daily chore of fetching water for their homes from distant public fountains.

a5183.speaker: Representative of the prefecture (Mahdi Adaweh)
a5183.speech: Welcomed a vital project of a social character, saying that bringing drinking water closer to households is the dream of every family and that it is coming true for dozens of families in the neighbourhood.

a5183.speaker: Daoud Said Gueldon, Vice-president of the regional council of Ali-Sabieh
a5183.speech: Congratulated the IFTIN association for this noble action facilitating the lives of many individuals, said collaboration between Civil Society Organisations and the Regional Council is imperative for regional development, and warmly thanked the donor, none other than USAID, the American agency for international cooperation.

a5183.speaker: Neighbourhood chief and other representatives of the IFTIN residential sector
a5183.speech: Welcomed the initiative favourably, as it goes in the direction of improving the living conditions of the population.

a5266.speaker: Media consultant to United Airlines (statement)
a5266.speech: A statement by the media consultant to the airline said the company is creating an aircraft design that has the potential to deliver jet fuel efficiency and a greatly enhanced customer experience; the investment includes a path to order up to 100 airplanes and an option for an additional 100, the statement said.

a5266.speaker: U.S. Air Force
a5266.speech: In 2023, the U.S. Air Force announced a $235 million contract to JetZero to fast-track the development of JetZero's full scale demonstrator.

a5266.speaker: Andrew Chang, Head of United Airlines Ventures (UAV)
a5266.speech: Said that if successful, JetZero has the potential to evolve the airline's core mainline business by developing aircraft with a bigger, more comfortable cabin experience for its customers, while increasing fuel efficiency across our network. "United Airlines Ventures was created to support our efforts to find innovative companies that can enhance the customer travel experience and help the airline lower its carbon footprint, and we believe JetZero reflects that philosophy," he added.

a5266.speaker: Tom O'Leary, Chief Executive Officer (CEO), JetZero
a5266.speech: Said United's investment in its company signaled the industry's belief that new, innovative technology was needed in order to achieve the efficiency and cost savings that would be required to meet the continued growth in demand for air travel across the globe. "JetZero is focused on one key technology - the airframe - that enables us to address all of the barriers to growth. This program is the only one in development today that promises efficiency and an elevated customer experience," he added.

a5479.speaker: Daniel Chapo, Mozambican President
a5479.speech: Revealed today at a joint press conference that Mozambique and Tanzania committed themselves to establishing a One-Stop Border Post at Negomano, Mueda district, Cabo Delgado: "At the end of the talks, we signed three legal instruments aimed at cementing the vast cooperation we have maintained since our independence, and even before independence until today."

a5479.speaker: Daniel Chapo, Mozambican President
a5479.speech: Highlighted the memorandum of understanding on the higher education student exchange programme, stating that both countries have been working for several years in this area, "and we think it was important for us to return to this cooperation on the exchange of higher education students between Mozambique and Tanzania" ; also referred to the agreement on the transfer of prisoners and memoranda of understanding on cooperation in culture, quality control of medicines and between Radio Mozambique and Tanzanian Radio.

a5479.speaker: Daniel Chapo, Mozambican President
a5479.speech: "Beyond these aspects, we reiterated the interest in holding periodic good-neighbourliness meetings between the neighbouring provinces of Niassa and Cabo Delgado, on the Mozambican side, and the provinces of Rovuma and Mtwara, on the Tanzanian side."

a5479.speaker: Daniel Chapo, Mozambican President
a5479.speech: Underlined the importance of establishing an association of cashew nut producing countries, as one of the sectors to be leveraged in trade cooperation, stating that it is pertinent that trade between Mozambique and Tanzania grow ever more.

a5479.speaker: Daniel Chapo, Mozambican President
a5479.speech: Made known that more than 20 years ago Mozambique began prospecting for natural gas in the districts of Inhassoro and Panda, Inhambane province, the existence of the roughly 820-kilometre pipeline from Temane to the South African city of Secunda led by Sasol, and the Coral Sul FLNG platform led by Eni off Palma district: "That is why we think this experience is also important to be passed on to our Tanzanian brothers, who are also working in this direction at the moment. Tanzania's wealth is Mozambique's wealth, and Mozambique's wealth is Tanzania's wealth, because we are all brothers and we think the exchange of experience is very important between brother countries."

a5625.speaker: Michael Gonzales, US Ambassador to Zambia
a5625.speech: Said this "difficult" decision was taken after repeated warnings to the Zambian government to safeguard vital drugs meant for the country's most vulnerable patients ; "We are no longer willing to underwrite the personal enrichment of fraudsters or the corrupt when patients go without or have to buy life-saving medications that we have provided for free."

a5625.speaker: Zambian government
a5625.speech: Said it had taken measures to tackle the issue.

a5625.speaker: Elijah Muchima, Zambian Health Minister
a5625.speech: Thanked the US for its "generous support", while saying that the problem of theft predated the current government which took office in 2021.

a5625.speaker: US embassy in Zambia (statement)
a5625.speech: Said the US accounts for about a third of public health spending in Zambia ; said officials had discovered the "country-wide theft" of medical products that were intended to be distributed for free to the public and were now being sold by private pharmacies; more than 2,000 pharmacies across Zambia were found selling donated drugs and medical supplies in a year-long investigation conducted by the US embassy ; "Shockingly, across these visits, 95 percent of the pharmacies that were selling the kinds of products that the United States provides, were also selling stolen goods." ; nearly half of the pharmacies visited were found selling medication and supplies donated by the US government, and other pharmacies were also selling stolen medical stocks purchased by the Zambian government, the Global Fund, and other donors.

a5625.speaker: US embassy in Zambia (statement)
a5625.speech: Said it had presented its findings and offered experts to help stop further theft and bring the culprits to justice in April last year but no action was taken: "I regret that to date, the government's actions have fallen drastically short of demonstrating a commitment to safeguarding US assistance and the lives we aim to save" ; said Zambia's law enforcement operations have focused on "low-level actors" and have led to the arrest of "only a few mid-level officials" instead of investigating supply sources and pursuing the masterminds behind the theft of medicines.

a5625.speaker: Michael Gonzales, US Ambassador to Zambia
a5625.speech: Said the US "can no longer justify to the American taxpayer continuing to provide such massive levels of assistance" ; said the cuts would affect drugs to treat malaria, HIV and TB ; "This is not a decision we have taken lightly", shedding tears as he explained how the measure would affect Zambian patients ; said the cuts would take effect January next year to give the Zambian government time to develop alternative arrangements but that "the decision had been made".

a5625.speaker: Elijah Muchima, Zambian Health Minister
a5625.speech: Said in response that "an advanced digital stock tracking system" had been set up to help monitor supplies of medicines, and reassured Zambians that there were sufficient stocks of all drugs so there was "no immediate risk of shortages".

a5625.speaker: Hakainde Hichilema, President of Zambia
a5625.speech: Said in March that Trump had "slapped us on both cheeks", saying it was time for his country to strengthen its treasury to procure its own medicines.

a5654.speaker: Mlotshwa, 32, researcher at the Antiviral Gene Therapy Research Unit, University of the Witwatersrand
a5654.speech: “This was very exciting. We were getting quite good results,” she told Reuters in the lab.

a5654.speaker: US State Department
a5654.speech: Did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

a5654.speaker: Nigel Garrett, chief scientific officer at the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation
a5654.speech: “It feels like you're building something and you could really make a huge difference” ; “And then it's wiped away.”

a5704.speaker: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Malawi
a5704.speech: says it is in discussion with the South African government over Pretoria’s decision to introduce visa requirements for Malawians holding service passports; on Wednesday, the ministry announced that Malawi service passport holders will be required to apply for visa before travel to South Africa effective October 16 2025 while ordinary and diplomatic passport holders are exempted.

a5704.speaker: George Chaponda, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Malawi
a5704.speech: in an interview yesterday said the Malawi High Commission in South Africa is leading the process; but he said the Malawi Government is not in a position to divulge details of the discussions at the moment ; “We are not in a position to comment on the matter until we have finished discussions.”

a5704.speaker: Department of Immigration and Citizenship Services (website / on record)
a5704.speech: Information on the website indicates that service passports are issued to senior government officials from Grade H and above, including directors, principal officers and heads of departments; the Department is on record to have indicated that 4,912 Malawians were deported from South Africa between January and June this year.

a5704.speaker: An Immigration Department source (anonymous)
a5704.speech: said applicants for service passports are required to present a letter from their ministries or departments confirming their employment status and grade; indicated that the service passports ensure smooth travel for the officers when they are going to carry out official duties; said earlier this year some people presented themselves as government officials and tried to apply for a service passport using forged letters purported to have been sourced from one of the ministries, and that the applications were rejected.

a5704.speaker: Pasqually Zulu, Immigration Department national spokesperson
a5704.speech: said he was in a meeting and did not pick up subsequent calls.

a5704.speaker: Chimwemwe Tsitsi, political and international relations analyst
a5704.speech: said the requirement for visas for service passports, while exempting ordinary passports, is surprising as one would have expected the opposite ; “But it is normal for countries to require travellers to have proper documents and be subjected to further scrutiny before travelling to that country.”

a5784.speaker: Former senior State Department official (anonymous)
a5784.speech: Said: “I sat down with people from the White House, and they asked: ‘What if we just let [Somalia] burn? Can we contain it?’ I said ‘No!’”

a5784.speaker: White House official (anonymous)
a5784.speech: Acknowledged growing frustration with the Somali government: “We are concerned about President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s prioritization of internal politics over counterterrorism efforts, particularly in light of the growing threat from al-Shabab,” the official told The Washington Post.

a5784.speaker: State Department press office
a5784.speech: Said the United States “will continue to work closely with Somali and African Union forces.”

a5784.speaker: Turkish officials
a5784.speech: Did not respond to requests for comment.

a5784.speaker: Former senior State Department official (anonymous)
a5784.speech: Said U.S. disengagement could fuel al-Shabab’s expansion into neighboring Kenya and Ethiopia and allow the Somali fighters to strengthen fledgling relations with Yemen’s Houthi rebels; said the last of two recent meetings between al-Shabab and the Houthis involved the Houthis sending an explosives expert to Jilib, al-Shabab’s de facto capital, citing U.S. intelligence.

a5784.speaker: U.N. sanctions experts
a5784.speech: Documented two recent meetings between al-Shabab and the Houthis.

a5784.speaker: Officials and diplomats (anonymous)
a5784.speech: Said any further American pullback could exacerbate Somalia’s political divisions and imperil efforts to contain one of the continent’s most acute security threats.

a5784.speaker: Larry Andre, former U.S. ambassador
a5784.speech: Said: “Things always start off great with a new president, and then clan politics makes it all fall apart,” recalling coordinating outfits with the beleaguered prime minister in 2022 during a joint news conference — their matching sky-blue running suits signaled they were united, Andre said, after political rivalries sparked deadly clan battles.

a5784.speaker: Hussein Sheikh Ali, Somalia’s national security adviser
a5784.speech: Said the U.S. helps organize Somalia’s seven core security partners, which include Britain, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and the African Union; all are against al-Shabab, Ali said, but sometimes have competing agendas: “On areas of counterterrorism [the Americans] are our lead partner.”

a5784.speaker: White House official (anonymous)
a5784.speech: Said American officials have “repeatedly urged” Mohamud “to refocus on security cooperation and regional inclusion, and are disappointed by the lack of progress,” and that his emphasis on centralizing power “is hindering progress on counterterrorism,” adding “and we believe a shift in priorities is essential to address the escalating threat.”

a5784.speaker: Aldebaran, risk consultancy company
a5784.speech: According to the consultancy, since February insurgents have taken back dozens of villages, including the strategic town of Adan Yabaal, and regained the ability to operate in nearly a third of the territory they lost to federal forces in 2022.

a5784.speaker: U.S. government audit (last year)
a5784.speech: Found that Danab had padded food and fuel requisitions.

a5784.speaker: Marco Rubio, U.S. Secretary of State
a5784.speech: Has said the wider freeze on foreign assistance programs will reduce government bloat and allow the administration to focus on domestic priorities.

a5784.speaker: Some former U.S. officials (anonymous)
a5784.speech: Say the torrent of international security funds into Somalia only fuels the country’s deep-rooted corruption; others contend that continued funding to a small, select unit working alongside U.S. soldiers is the best among bad options.

a5784.speaker: Former senior U.S. military official (anonymous)
a5784.speech: Said: “If we don’t directly sustain the Danab, the Somali National Army is highly unlikely to sustain them to the degree required for them to be most effective.”

a5784.speaker: Mogadishu-based security expert who works with the Somali military (anonymous)
a5784.speech: Said morale within Danab is “not that high”; when the stipends were cut, about 100 soldiers “went AWOL for a bit,” he said, and most of Danab’s foreign mentors also went home after the U.S. cuts.

a5784.speaker: U.S. security officials (anonymous)
a5784.speech: Said plans to deploy the roughly 500 U.S. forces in Somalia across the country to better support Danab are also under review now.

a5784.speaker: Senior Somali security official (anonymous)
a5784.speech: Said an April 16 U.S. airstrike on two unflagged vessels off the Somali coast hit a shipment of surface-to-air missiles from Yemen.

a5784.speaker: U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM)
a5784.speech: Declined to provide details, but its news release said the boat carried “advanced conventional weapons.”

a5784.speaker: Western military official (anonymous)
a5784.speech: Said: “Airstrikes are only useful if you have good ground troops to hold.”

a5784.speaker: Former senior U.S. military official (anonymous)
a5784.speech: Said AFRICOM has seen the spending and the risk to U.S. forces as an acceptable cost to contain a potential threat; noted that U.S. access to the Horn of Africa has decreased steadily over the past decade: “The accountant’s argument might be we hand [Somalia] off to the Turks and let them handle that security problem, but the cost of reentry is significant, and we lose influence over key geographic terrain,” ; “When you sacrifice that and burden-shift it to an ally … it’s unlikely your interests and objectives will align.”

a5784.speaker: Berkay Mandiraci, senior analyst for Turkey at the International Crisis Group
a5784.speech: Said: “With traditional powers retreating from parts of Africa, Ankara sees an opportunity to step in. Somalia holds strategic value for Ankara, sitting astride key shipping lanes and vital trade routes.”

a5784.speaker: Mogadishu-based diplomat (anonymous)
a5784.speech: Said of Turkish operations, which other partners say they are often not informed about: “At times you had multiple UAVs over a target,” using the abbreviation for unmanned aerial vehicles.

a5784.speaker: Witnesses (in Somalia)
a5784.speech: Told The Post that Turkish strikes from less-powerful drones have killed at least 40 civilians since late 2022.

a5784.speaker: Witnesses and a relative
a5784.speech: Said a January 2023 strike on a gathering under a tree killed seven civilians, including an 8-year-old, in the town of Quracley.

a5784.speaker: A local doctor
a5784.speech: Said eight were killed on Sept. 9, 2022, when a strike hit a group of drivers and hawkers in the al-Shabab-controlled town of Mubarak.

a5784.speaker: Mohamed Nur Ahmed, 50, who lost three sons and a nephew in the Quracley strike
a5784.speech: Said: “I couldn’t even wash my children’s bodies according to the Islamic custom,” because they were “ripped to pieces.”

a5784.speaker: Western diplomat (anonymous)
a5784.speech: Said: “You’ve got the Somalis telling the Turks to … save Mogadishu at all costs. This will inevitably lead to further civilian casualties, which can be exploited by al-Shabab.”

a5784.speaker: Larry Andre, former U.S. ambassador
a5784.speech: Said: “Somalia is resource rich, but insecurity has prevented the commercialization of those resources. If we desert our partners, then others will replace us and reap the rewards when Somalia establishes peace and prosperity.”

a5797.speaker: Nangolo Mbumba, President of Namibia
a5797.speech: Says Namibia’s ongoing drought should be seen as a motivation for irrigation schemes to receive the full support they would need from the government. “We should use this drought as a springboard to make sure that we truly pay attention to our green schemes. To put in the necessary funds and to motivate those who are working to make sure that they produce.” ; “The cabinet decided a long time ago to make sure that we give the minister of agriculture enough resources to make sure that our green schemes truly become green. To get their tractors, get their machinery, get their seeds, get their fertilisers.” ; Said he is encouraged by the efforts, saying the country is on the right track, especially when it comes to the ministry of agriculture availing more resources to the irrigation projects.

a5797.speaker: Nangolo Mbumba, President of Namibia
a5797.speech: “I have never been to the blueberry farm. It is also to encourage investors who want to invest in our land. We have enough land. We have water; the soil is deep enough. For them to expand their production and for others to come and invest in our countries to create jobs.”

a5797.speaker: Nangolo Mbumba, President of Namibia
a5797.speech: “It is very important that Namibians start taking care of themselves. As Dr. Nujoma long ago said, The nation that cannot feed itself cannot possibly be proud of its own existence, so we have to be proud, do things in our own country, and take decisions that may be difficult, but they are our decisions.”

a5797.speaker: Farm manager, Uvhungu-Vhungu Irrigation project (Kavango East)
a5797.speech: Presented the farm’s performance and some of the difficulties experienced; one of the major concerns is that, despite the fact that the wheat is ready for harvesting, the green scheme does not have its own combine harvester.

a5929.speaker: Linda Bezuidenhout, Tanzanian fashion designer living in the United States
a5929.speech: “I am a fashion designer and very proud of my Wazaramo heritage. It is in me even here in the US” ; said her passion to ensure her designs reach global mileage motivated her to pursue her modeling career in the US.

a5929.speaker: Linda Bezuidenhout, Tanzanian fashion designer living in the United States
a5929.speech: Said she started her fashion design career at a tender age: “I was only eight years old then” ; said her mother, who was a member of a tailoring group, was her biggest influence in her fashion design career: “She used to give me a free choice on how to make my dress; therefore, I used to design it myself before my mother made it perfectly to my design.”

a5929.speaker: Linda Bezuidenhout, Tanzanian fashion designer living in the United States
a5929.speech: “I feel obliged to design something big for our beloved president, Dr Samia Suuhu Hassan, and I hope to make something very Tanzanian for her.”

a5929.speaker: Linda Bezuidenhout, Tanzanian fashion designer living in the United States
a5929.speech: On her organization’s humanitarian assistance: “I have done it well in those areas, but I can’t mention the areas or people whom I helped since it is not good in our religion.”

a6540.speaker: Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
a6540.speech: States that one of the reasons why PrEP is less effective is usually when it is not taken as prescribed.

a6540.speaker: Mutafela Muhapi, Project Hope Namibia (PHN)
a6540.speech: Said a project like DREAMS is doing well in educating the targeted group of 10 to 14 year olds, even though there is still a large number that is not in the know; “Accessibility to PrEP is not difficult as it requires one to get tested first before getting. After getting tested, there is what we call healthcare assistance, the people who do testing at the clinics”; said at DREAMS they also do testing and they are certified antiretroviral therapy nurses, which means they can prescribe PrEP and PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis).

a6540.speaker: Mutafela Muhapi, Project Hope Namibia (PHN)
a6540.speech: Said healthcare workers should take it upon themselves to spread the right information to individuals seeking PrEP: “I have heard girls seeking PrEP that they were told by health professionals the medication is for sex workers only and you still hear others who go for private doctors if they are asked if they are on any other treatment and they say PrEP, they get told that they are on ARV, the mood changes. Yes PrEP is a type of an ARV but the main aim is for prevention”; said this becomes tricky as confusion is created among nurses and doctors.

a6540.speaker: Mutafela Muhapi, Project Hope Namibia (PHN)
a6540.speech: Added: “Some people think PrEP disturbs one’s menstrual cycle, this is not the case. It has nothing to do with that, they maybe think it will hinder the process of family planning”; added that common side effects include nausea and drowsiness, which is why she recommends that PrEP is somehow best taken at night when one’s about to sleep.

a6760.speaker: Sylvestre Fandohan, technical adviser to Benin's Minister of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries
a6760.speech: Believes the cashew value chain deserves to be developed and put in the spotlight, taking into account all the actors, from nursery operators to processors of cashew nuts and cashew apples, including producers, without overlooking the institutions involved in its development ; said the government has mobilized substantial resources with the help of its technical and financial partners, among them the US Department of Agriculture, through the BeninCaju project implemented with the technical support of the international NGO TechnoServe in partnership with Catholic Relief Services (CRS) ; added that the establishment of the Glo-Djigbe Industrial Zone (GDIZ) considerably increases local nut processing capacity and thus offers new prospects for the flourishing of the sector.

a6760.speaker: Soule Manigui, deputy country director of TechnoServe Benin
a6760.speech: "Benin's cashew sector has very significant potential, but one that still remains little developed."

a6760.speaker: Epitace Nobera, chief of mission of the BeninCaju project
a6760.speech: Said Benin has seen progressive growth in production and processing over recent years ; praises the contribution of research through the development of high-performing planting material, the training of nursery operators, actors' access to financing, talent development, and technological innovations such as CajuLabs, several achievements that will be the subject of sharing and exchange.

a6799.speaker: State prosecutors (Liberia) — notice of exception filed to the court
a6799.speech: Challenged the legality of the US$8 million property bond, pointing out discrepancies related to the ownership and evaluation of the properties listed in the bond, with one property flagged for an outstanding tax lien; highlighted that the properties listed may not meet legal standards even if they were properly assessed and unencumbered, and raised concerns about the bond's coverage since Mr. Tweah's criminal appearance bond is already being used as surety in another case involving co-defendant Stanley Ford ; “The properties as contained in the statement of property evaluation and the Real Estate Tax Demand Notice and the Real Property Tax Division's state of property evaluation, are purportedly owned by Rudolph S. Cole and Refina J. Cole” ; argued that even if the properties were properly listed and unencumbered, they would still not meet legal standards because “the bond ought to be twice the amount embezzled in addition to the maximum number of months of imprisonment multiplied by US$25”; are seeking to disqualify the property with identification number 33933 due to an outstanding tax lien of US$23,737.80.

a6799.speaker: Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA)
a6799.speech: Reports no records to substantiate the ownership or value assessment for the properties listed, specifically property identification number 25115.

a6799.speaker: Dorbor Jallah, LRA Commissioner General (communication to Solicitor General Cllr. Augustine Fayiah)
a6799.speech: “The property with identification number 33933 with property valuation of US$6,000,000.00 does not currently exist in the LRA's system” ; “It is also observed that the US$6,000,000.00 was initially imputed into the system on February 17, 2023, and attracted a tax bill of US$15,000. It was subsequently voided and reinputted at the value of US$600,000.00 with a tax bill of US$1,500.” ; “Randolph S. Cole and Rafina J. Cole's property is yet to be identified and assessed by the valuation section of the Real Estate Tax Division since it was discovered on February 20, 2023 when the US$6,000,000 was inputted into the system on February 17, 2023.”

a6799.speaker: Samuel D. Tweah, former Finance Minister of Liberia
a6799.speech: Has denied the charges of economic sabotage, fraud, and criminal conspiracy, attributing them to what he perceives as politically motivated persecution orchestrated by the Unity Party-led government; expressed confidence in the judicial process despite the legal challenges he faces; said he stands firm and resolute to answer to the charges brought against him and four other former top officials who served in the immediate past government; in a social media post on Thursday said that he returned to Liberia to confront the allegations, voicing his determination to face the legal proceedings and challenge what he perceives as politically motivated accusations by the current administration; affirmed his innocence and emphasized his unwavering commitment to returning to Liberia under lawful circumstances to fight the charges against him.

a6874.speaker: Aid agencies
a6874.speech: have said the world's youngest country, highly vulnerable to climate change, is in the grip of its worst flooding in decades, mainly in the north.

a6874.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) (statement)
a6874.speech: said on Friday that the floods have affected about 1.4 million people across 43 counties and the disputed Abyei region, which is claimed by both South Sudan and Sudan; added in a statement that more than 379,000 people were displaced in 22 counties and in Abyei ; “A surge in malaria has been reported in Jonglei, Unity, Upper Nile, Northern Bahr el Ghazal, Central Equatoria and Western Equatoria states – overwhelming the health system and exacerbating the situation and impact in flood-hit areas.”

a6874.speaker: World Bank
a6874.speech: said last month that the latest floods were “worsening an already critical humanitarian situation marked by severe food insecurity, economic decline, continued conflict, disease outbreaks, and the repercussions of the Sudan conflict”.

a6874.speaker: UN's World Food Programme (WFP)
a6874.speech: According to the WFP, more than seven million people are food insecure in South Sudan and 1.65 million children are malnourished.

a6874.speaker: Office of the President of South Sudan
a6874.speech: announced in September yet another extension to a transitional period agreed to in a 2018 peace deal, delaying elections by two years to December 2026.

a7019.speaker: Claver Gatete, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a7019.speech: Warned that, with Africa’s public debt having reached 1,860 billion dollars, more than 20 African countries are already over-indebted or on the verge of being so; revealed that Africa’s total public debt would reach 1,860 billion dollars in 2024 and that the average debt-to-GDP ratio rose from 44.4% in 2015 to 66.7% today ; “When debt service exceeds combined investment in health and education, it is legitimate to question the sustainability of our fiscal trajectory, as well as its human cost.”

a7019.speaker: Claver Gatete, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a7019.speech: Stressed that Africa faces increasingly limited access to concessional financing while rising customs barriers hinder the export of its products, resulting in higher borrowing costs, declining revenues and ever tighter fiscal margins ; “Africa is not only facing a debt crisis. It is a genuine development crisis, in which debt payments compete directly with vital priorities such as health, education, infrastructure and the fundamental right to development.”

a7019.speaker: Claver Gatete, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a7019.speech: Stressed that the traditional international financing on which the continent relied, notably official development assistance, is drying up, indicating by way of example that 83% of USAID’s programmes have been cancelled while Africa’s historical partners tighten their own budgets.

a7019.speaker: Claver Gatete, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a7019.speech: Deplored the dizzying increase in the cost of capital and the lack of effectiveness of the G20 Common Framework, judged slow, opaque and too favourable to creditors.
